tfn.s: Tom Kerridge does not believe parents who say their children eat beetroot and feta salad.
tfn.why: The text says: “He does not believe the parents who say their children happily eat beetroot and feta salad.”

tfn.s: Helen Goh hides vegetables without telling her children.
tfn.why: The text says: “she always tells her sons it is in there.”

tfn.s: Ravneet Gill does not describe sugar as a treat.
tfn.why: The text says: “She does not call it a treat.”

tfn.s: Tom Kerridge's son, Acey, is five years old.
tfn.why: The text says Acey is ten. The five-year-old is Marie Mitchell's daughter.

tfn.s: Most of the nine cooks eat with their children every day.
tfn.why: Not stated. The text says nothing about how often they eat together.

focus.note: A phrasal verb is a verb plus a small word, such as out or on. The small word changes the meaning, so learn the two words together.

items.s: Most children grow ____ of fussy eating.

The chefs say you should carry ____ offering a food, even after a refusal.
Parents who welcome a child's ____ in the cooking, by letting her stir or wash the vegetables, often see less refusal at the table.
Offering two sensible choices at snack time gives a toddler a sense of ____ over what she eats.
Hiding broccoli in a smoothie is a popular ____ for getting children to eat vegetables, though some chefs object to it.
My neighbour's ____ words, that every toddler goes through this, made me feel less alone.

tfn.s: Tom Kerridge's way of dealing with hunger is to feed his son early.
tfn.why: The text says he gets food in front of Acey “before hunger turns into a request for whatever comes in the brightest wrapper.”

tfn.s: Anna Jones always refuses to make a second meal for a child.
tfn.why: The text says she “cannot bring herself to send a child to bed hungry, so she does make alternatives.”

tfn.s: Helen Goh and Marie Mitchell both think a child should know what is in her food.
tfn.why: Goh “tells her sons exactly what is in it” and Mitchell says a child who does not know “will never discover that she likes it.”

tfn.s: Ravneet Gill's parents used sugar as a reward when she was a child.
tfn.why: The text says things went wrong for her as a child, but not how her parents used sugar.

tfn.s: All of Margot Henderson's children are under thirty.
tfn.why: The text says her children are “in their late twenties and thirties.”

focus.note: Many phrasal verbs have a meaning you cannot guess from the two words, so learn the whole verb. The same verb with a different small word means something new: give in, give up.

tfn.s: Marie Mitchell and Helen Goh both reject hiding vegetables, but not for the same reason.
tfn.why: Goh does not want food to become “a trick”, while Mitchell's objection is that a child who never knows what she ate “cannot learn what she likes.”

tfn.s: According to the article, Anna Jones's eldest son began eating widely after he learned about nutrition.
tfn.why: The text says it followed Japanese food entering his imagination “through stories about ninjas.”

tfn.s: Tom Kerridge's son eats a wider range of food than most ten-year-olds.
tfn.why: The text says only that “His own son eats well”, with no comparison to other children.

tfn.s: The writer treats the nine households as a representative sample of parents.
tfn.why: The text calls them “nine individual households” and “none of them a sample.”

tfn.s: Jackson Boxer and Rosie Birkett both had to separate their own feelings from their children's refusals.
tfn.why: Boxer stopped taking refusal personally, and Birkett “had to separate her ego from what they were asking for.”

focus.note: At this level, learn phrasal verbs that carry a formal or abstract meaning, such as rule out, single out and boil down to. Check whether the verb needs an object and where it goes.

speak.title: Role-play: to hide it or to tell her?
speak.setup: Work in pairs. Read your card, then have the conversation. Swap roles and do it again.

a.role: the parent who wants to hide it
a.text: Your four-year-old will not eat vegetables. You want to grate courgette into the pasta sauce and say nothing. Explain why, and try to agree on a plan.

b.role: the parent who wants to tell her
b.text: You think your daughter should know what is in her food. Explain why, listen to your partner, and try to agree on a plan you both like.

phrases: That's a good point, but I'm not sure it's fair.
She won't learn what she likes if she never knows.
How about we try both ways?
I think we're worrying too much.
speak.after: Tell the class what you agreed, and whether either of you changed your mind.
